sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: high versus low beams, braking with and without ABS, brake failure versus stuck pedal, blowout versus shoulder drift, regulatory versus advisory work-zone signs, plus continuation facts on night crashes, weather, wipers, headlights, disabled vehicles, floods and shoulder use
Confusable pairs among the special-conditions rules, followed by continuation facts that did not fit part C; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec08-R01 | anchor: A01
High beams belong in open country at night, but you must dim to low beams at least 500 feet before an oncoming vehicle and at least 300 feet behind a vehicle you follow. [A01]
Why it matters: group headlights; confusable five hundred versus three hundred feet.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-R02 | anchor: A01
Pedestrians are hard to see at night, so stay especially watchful for them after dark. [A01]
Why it matters: group night driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-R03 | anchor: A01
Between 2015 and 2019 Nevada recorded 276 fatal crashes from 6:00 PM to 8:59 PM, which was 19% of all fatal crashes. [A01]
Why it matters: group night driving; historical statistic; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-R04 | anchor: A02
Nevada weather can change suddenly with wind, rain and snowstorms, and in fog, rain or snow other drivers struggle to see just as you do, so leave extra space and watch the tail lights ahead. [A02]
Why it matters: group bad weather; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-R05 | anchor: A02
Without ABS, brake on ice with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern, while with ABS you hold firm, continuous pressure on the pedal; check the owner's manual. [A02]
Why it matters: group bad weather; confusable braking with versus without ABS.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-R06 | anchor: A02
On snow and ice avoid sudden changes in speed or direction, keep windows and windshield clear, and allow extra time to reach your destination. [A02]
Why it matters: group bad weather; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-R07 | anchor: A02
Skid recovery differs by braking and steering system and by four-wheel or front-wheel drive, so the owner's manual is the source for your vehicle, and in any emergency stay calm. [A02]
Why it matters: group skids; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-R08 | anchor: A03
With failed brakes you shift to a lower gear and use the parking brake, while with a stuck gas pedal you shift to neutral and brake; in neither case do you shift into park. [A03]
Why it matters: group emergencies; confusable brake failure versus stuck pedal.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-R09 | anchor: A03
Use a lower gear when driving downhill for long stretches to avoid wearing out the brakes. [A03]
Why it matters: group emergencies; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-R10 | anchor: A03
When the wipers stop working during heavy rain or snow, reduce speed, roll the window down and lean out to see, and get off the highway to the right and stop as soon as you can. [A03]
Why it matters: group emergencies; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-R11 | anchor: A03
If the headlights fail, slow down and leave the roadway as soon as possible, using parking lights, turn signals or four-way flashers, which usually still work, to guide you. [A03]
Why it matters: group emergencies; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-R12 | anchor: A04
In a blowout you must not hit the brakes until the vehicle is under control, whereas after drifting onto the shoulder you may brake, but only carefully; in both cases grip the wheel firmly and lift off the gas. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; confusable blowout versus shoulder drift.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-R13 | anchor: A04
After a blowout, signal, pull safely off the road and warn others with parking lights or flashers. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-R14 | anchor: A04
With a disabled vehicle, get all four wheels off the roadway if possible, warn other drivers with parking lights, flashers or flares, and have it towed as soon as you can. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-R15 | anchor: A04
Nevada's dry climate makes flash floods likely, especially in summer storms, spring thaw or long rains, and floating vehicles drift toward deeper, faster water where top-heavy ones may roll. [A04]
Why it matters: group flash floods; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-R16 | anchor: A05
Be extra careful about floods at night, never cross flowing streams or water over the road, and when water rises fast turn around and move to higher ground away from creeks and flood channels. [A05]
Why it matters: group flash floods; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-R17 | anchor: A05
A black and white speed limit sign in a work zone is the legal limit, while an orange one is only an advisory, safer speed. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; confusable regulatory versus advisory signs.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-R18 | anchor: A05
Visibility in work zones may be lower, especially at night, so do not drive tired and watch for sleepy drivers; flaggers and pilot cars often control traffic. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-R19 | anchor: A06
Some emergency vehicles may drive on a paved highway shoulder where signs authorize it, including police, fire engines and ambulances, traffic incident management vehicles, tow cars, coroner vehicles and public transit buses (NRS 484B.210). [A06]
Why it matters: group shoulders; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-R20 | anchor: A06
The shoulder-use rule for emergency vehicles took effect on January 1, 2024. [A06]
Why it matters: group shoulders; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0061]
